title: First-time buyer mortgage sales fell across London in decade to 2023
meta_description: London is no longer the top location for UK first-time mortgage buyers, as new homeowners purchase homes in more rural and affordable locations.

breadcrumb.text: First-time buyer mortgage sales fell across London in decade to 2023

lede: First-time mortgage buyers bought homes further from the capital compared to 10 years earlier, ONS analysis of Financial Conduct Authority data show.

body.text: 18 March 2025

body.box_text: Notice, 19 March 2025: The proportion of first-time buyer mortgages sold in London in 2023 has been corrected to 12.8%. It was previously reported as 12.7% in the section titled 'London no longer the top location for first-time buyer mortgages'.

body.text: Several London boroughs saw some of the largest falls in the rate of first-time buyer mortgage sales in the UK between 2013 and 2023.

This is according to ONS analysis of [data from the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/housing/datasets/firsttimebuyermortgagesalesbylocalauthorityuk2006to2023), which have been published at local authority level for the first time.
Similar trends can be seen in other major cities across the UK, with rates of first-time buyer mortgage sales falling or growing more slowly than surrounding areas.
Overall, the South East saw a higher share of new first-time buyer mortgages than London in 2023, with the largest growth in the North East of England and Northern Ireland.

The FCA data show that the overall number of new first-time buyer mortgages in the UK has been falling since the peak in 2021, and in 2023 was the lowest since 2013, at 282,000. However, sales of first-time buyer mortgages made up a greater proportion of total residential property sales in 2023 (38.4%) than they did 10 years before (28.0%).
FCA data used in this article and in the accompanying dataset relates specifically to first-time buyer mortgage sales and does not include cash buyers.

We have presented the number of first-time buyer mortgage sales per 1,000 dwellings as it adjusts for the size of each local authority. This is a fairer measure to see local trends and allows a better comparison. You can also see the number of first-time buyer mortgage sales per 100 home sales and the exact number of first-time buyer mortgage sales for each local authority on the map below.

body.h2: London no longer the top location for first-time buyer mortgages
body.text: In 2023, 12.8% of first-time buyer mortgages were sold for homes located in the capital – down from 16.8% a decade earlier.

body.h2: London no longer the top location for first-time buyer mortgages
body.text: The South East of England had the highest proportion of first-time buyer mortgages in the UK in 2023 at 13.8%.

body.h2: London no longer the top location for first-time buyer mortgages
body.text: Of the 10 areas with the highest rates of first-time buyer mortgages per 1,000 dwellings in 2023, one was in London, compared with six in 2013.

body.h2: London no longer the top location for first-time buyer mortgages
body.text: Between 2013 and 2021, when first-time buyer mortgage sales peaked, only 10 local authorities saw falls in the rate of first-time buyer mortgage sales, eight of which were London boroughs.

body.h2: In Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, areas with the fastest growth in first-time buyer mortgages were often outside major cities

body.h2: In Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, areas with the fastest growth in first-time buyer mortgages were often outside major cities
body.text: In the devolved administrations, the rate of first-time buyer mortgages is growing fastest in areas surrounding the metropolitan centres.

body.h2: In Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, areas with the fastest growth in first-time buyer mortgages were often outside major cities
body.text: The areas with the highest growth in the rate of first-time buyer mortgages in Scotland, (more than 35.0%) were South Lanarkshire, North and South Ayrshire, West Dunbartonshire and Renfrewshire.

body.h2: In Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, areas with the fastest growth in first-time buyer mortgages were often outside major cities
body.text: Metropolitan areas like Dundee City, Glasgow City and the City of Edinburgh saw slower growth, of 8.0%, 24.7% and 10.9% respectively.

body.h2: In Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, areas with the fastest growth in first-time buyer mortgages were often outside major cities
body.text: While Aberdeen City had the highest rate of first-time buyer mortgages in Scotland in 2013 (15.6 per 1,000), since then it fell to 10.8 per 1,000 in 2023. By 2023 the City of Edinburgh had the highest rate of first-time buyer mortgages, at 13.1 per 1,000 dwellings.

body.h2: In Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, areas with the fastest growth in first-time buyer mortgages were often outside major cities
body.text: In Wales, most areas saw growth in first-time buyer mortgage sales, with the highest in Newport and Torfaen, where rates grew more than 40.0% since 2013 to 12.8 per 1,000 and 10.7 per 1,000, respectively, in 2023.

body.h2: In Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, areas with the fastest growth in first-time buyer mortgages were often outside major cities
body.text: While Cardiff had the highest rate of first-time buyer mortgages in 2013 (9.7 per 1,000 dwellings), it grew more slowly over the following decade (8.6%) to 10.6 per 1,000.

body.h2: In Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, areas with the fastest growth in first-time buyer mortgages were often outside major cities
body.text: Belfast showed the strongest growth rates of the devolved capitals between 2013 and 2023 of 27.9% (to 10.3 per 1,000 dwellings), but Antrim and Newtownabbey saw higher growth in Northern Ireland of 37.7% to 13.7 per 1,000 dwellings in 2023.

body.h2: Fewer first-time buyers in England’s most urban areas
body.text: Fewer first-time buyers in England’s most urban areas

body.h2: Fewer first-time buyers in England’s most urban areas
body.text: While the rate of first-time buyer mortgage sales has been falling in London, they have risen in more rural areas.

body.h2: Fewer first-time buyers in England’s most urban areas
body.text: On average, rural areas in England and Wales saw rates of first-time buyer mortgages rise by 9.7% between 2013 and 2023, while urban areas saw a 3.7% rise on average.

body.h2: Fewer first-time buyers in England’s most urban areas
body.text: In 2013, all 20 areas with the highest rates of first-time buyer mortgages were urban, with the majority of the population near to a major town or city, [according to the 2021 urban rural classification](https://www.ons.gov.uk/methodology/geography/geographicalproducts/ruralurbanclassifications/2021ruralurbanclassification).

body.h2: Fewer first-time buyers in England’s most urban areas
body.text: However, as numbers of first-time buyer mortgage sales grew between 2013 and 2021, rural areas saw some of the highest growth rates (63.3% on average compared with an average of 48.8% across urban areas).

body.h2: Fewer first-time buyers in England’s most urban areas
body.text: The rate of first-time buyer mortgages in West Oxfordshire grew from 7.2 per 1,000 in 2013 to 16.6 per 1,000 in 2021, an increase of 131.8%, the highest of any local authority in this period.

body.h2: Fewer first-time buyers in England’s most urban areas
body.text: By 2021, three of the 20 areas in England and Wales with the highest rates of first-time buyer mortgages were ‘intermediate rural’, with the majority nearer to a major town or city. These were:

body.text: Central Bedfordshire (22.3 per 1,000 dwellings)

body.h2: Fewer first-time buyers in England’s most urban areas

body.h2: Fewer first-time buyers in England’s most urban areas

body.h2: Fewer first-time buyers in England’s most urban areas
body.text: Between 2021 and 2023, as first-time buyer mortgages sales began to fall, rates fell faster in rural areas (-32.3%) compared with urban areas (-30.1%).

body.h2: Fewer first-time buyers in England’s most urban areas
body.text: Those urban areas which saw the strongest growth in first-time buyer mortgage sales in the full decade between 2013 and 2023 were outside London, in:

body.h2: Fewer first-time buyers in England’s most urban areas
body.text: Harlow in the East of England (68.6%)

body.h2: Fewer first-time buyers in England’s most urban areas
body.text: Knowsley in the North West (63.3%)

body.h2: Fewer first-time buyers in England’s most urban areas
body.text: Nuneaton and Bedworth in the West Midlands (56.1%)

body.h2: Fewer first-time buyers in England’s most urban areas
body.text: A small number of local authorities in England and Wales could not be included in these urban-rural comparisons. This is because some local authorities have changed boundaries since they were classed as rural or urban from 2021 census data.

body.text: By looking back through nearly two decades-worth of data, we can see how certain events affected the number of first-time buyer mortgage sales.

body.text: For the available time series, the number of UK first-time buyer mortgages sold was relatively high in 2006, at around 377,000, but by the time of the 2008 global financial crisis two years later, that number had fallen by nearly half to 186,000.

body.h2: About the data
body.text: About the data

body.h2: About the data
body.text: The first-time buyer indicator in the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) data is reported by the mortgage providers and its definition may vary across firms. For example, individuals who are not remortgaging but have previously owned a property may or may not be counted as first-time buyers. Additionally, if a mortgage is taken out jointly by one first-time buyer and one non-first-time buyer, it may or may not be counted as a first-time buyer mortgage.

body.h2: About the data
body.text: The data in this release is presented at the local authority level in the United Kingdom, based on calendar years. The FCA publish data on the [number of first-time buyers at the country and regional level](https://www.fca.org.uk/data/product-sales-data/mortgages-dashboards) on a quarterly basis. When local authority counts are aggregated to form regional or country-level figures, the numbers of first-time buyers may differ. This discrepancy occurs for three reasons:

body.h2: About the data
body.text: The geographical matching process differs between data releases. To assign local authorities to PSD001 transactions, it is matched to the [National Statistics Postcode Lookup (NSPL)](https://geoportal.statistics.gov.uk/search?q=PRD_NSPL%20AUG_2024&sort=Date%20Created%7Ccreated%7Cdesc) by property postcode.

body.h2: About the data
body.text: The FCA’s Mortgages Product Sales Dataset (PSD001) is updated daily, incorporating new data submissions from firms, as well as resubmissions (where firms amend previously submitted data).

body.h2: About the data
body.text: Steps are taken to de-duplicate the data used in this publication

body.h2: About the data
body.text: Counts are redacted with the symbol ":" for any local authority and year where the number of first-time buyer mortgage sales is less than 10.
